turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Brennan. Jacket off, there, and we'll get the numbers done before Doctor Walsh is through.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning. Umm, we were nearly late, the card was in the other coat, and the lift is broken so we took the stairs, and the right knee nearly went on me on the second flight. Nora stays with me weeknights now, which is just as well, I'd have turned back home otherwise.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He'll give you the full bus timetable if you let him. Arm out straight, Tom.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure today is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Your last pressure was one-forty. Weight is fifty-two kilos. Last time in March you were sixty-eight.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Sixty-eight in March? Well, the clothes are looser, I'll give you that, but sixty-eight sounds like a different man entirely. Are you sure that's my line on the card and not the lad before me?
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): It's your card, I've checked. Temperature hopped up to thirty-seven, no, scratch that, it's thirty-eight point three. Pulse is sixty-four.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Mm. He didn't feel hot in the car. I had the back of my hand on his forehead at the lights.
[SEG0008] person_1 (NURSE): The machine has settled on thirty-eight point three, so that's what I'm writing down. Doctor won't be long.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tom, Nora. I'm after looking at the bloods from this morning. Creatinine is one hundred and forty-eight, and the eGFR is down at thirty-eight.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty-eight, right. The time before, in the hospital, they said it was borderline. Umm, the girl might have said forty-something, but I never wrote it down, it was the winter I had the chest, or the winter before, I couldn't put a date on it.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll stick with today's figure, not the memory of it. What brought you in, in your own words?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The kidney review, and the diabetes check. And the knees, if I'm being honest, the right one most of all. I've been buying the ibuprofen in the shop, the neurofen, even though I was told not to touch it.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): The shop ibuprofen. How many are you taking, and how long is that going on?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Two of the two-hundred milligram tablets, three times a day, with the tea. I started about six weeks ago, the day I was down on the floor at the washing machine and the right knee blew up on me. It's a dull ache, worse on the stairs, better if I sit and put the leg up, and I know well it's against the advice.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I told him to leave them in the press. My sister took the same yoke for her back for years and she ended up in Vincent's with a bleed, so I've no time for them.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the ramipril, you're still on five milligrams in the morning?

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): The ramapril, yes, five milligrams every morning, I don't miss it. The metformin is five hundred twice a day, breakfast and the tea, for the sugar, and I've had the diabetes eleven years, since I was sixty-four. The Beaumont doctor put me on the ramapril for the pressure and to mind the kidneys.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, no. And the breath is grand, I can walk to the shop. It's only the knee that stops me, and even then only on the stairs, not on the flat.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks, any burning or—
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He was up in the night, I heard him on the landing.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning, and no blood in it. I do get up once, sometimes twice, but that's years, not a new thing, it's the tea as much as anything. Sorry, you hadn't finished there.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's all I needed. Any allergies to medicines that you know of?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): None at all. I had penicillin for that chest and there was no rash, no trouble of any kind. My father had the sugar as well, though that's hardly an allergy, I'm rambling now.

[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking out loud. A creatinine of one forty-eight and an eGFR of thirty-eight is a real drop, and the ibuprofen off the shelf is the likely reason. It squeezes the little filters in the kidney, and the ramipril is already easing the vessel going in, so the two together can shove the numbers the wrong way.

[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll keep the ramipril at five milligrams every morning, and the metformin as you are on it. Don't stop either of those. The ibuprofen stops today, and for the knee it's paracetamol by mouth, one gram, two of the five-hundreds, up to four times in the day, and no more anti-inflammatories out of the shop.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): So the neurofen goes in the bin even if the knee is screaming. And eight paracetamol is the ceiling, the chemist wrote that on the old box, it's still on the fridge, the ink is faded but you can read the eight.

[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Eight is the ceiling, yes. And while I'm explaining, the diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet, so a sore can be well on before you feel a thing. Someone needs to look at those feet every night.
[SEG0029] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll do the feet. I do my own father's on a Sunday, he's ninety-one, though that's my day off and nothing to do with this job.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): They look all right when I check, I think. Umm, I do get a tingling in the toes at night, the last three months or so, pins and needles, mild, it comes and goes. I wasn't sure it was even worth mentioning, to be honest with you.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Worth mentioning. Right knee is warm, but there's no big swelling now. Both feet are warm, the pulses are there, the skin is intact. Ankles, no pitting.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any extra thirst? And the weight, were you trying to lose it? You've come down since March.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirst is the same as always, no change there. I wasn't trying to lose the weight at all. The appetite has been poor since the knee started, I leave half the dinner, Nora's spuds and all, and I didn't think it had come to that much.

[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Poor appetite, and weight you didn't mean to lose. I'll park that with the kidneys for now, though it may just be eating less with the pain, and I can't separate the two today, so no firmer label. Repeat creatinine and eGFR in two weeks, that's booked, and a urine dip before you leave, the nurse will catch you on the way out.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks is grand. Do I have to fast for it? The last time, before they even called it diabetes, they said the sugar was borderline, and I'd had a banana on the way in, so I never knew if that result even counted.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): No need to fast. If the repeat comes back worse we might refer you on to the kidney clinic, but that is not booked today.
[SEG0037] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put the two weeks in the phone. I've my own blood pressure clinic that Thursday for my tablets, so I'll swap the morning with the agency.

[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Ibuprofen stopped from today, paracetamol in its place, ramipril and metformin carried on, feet looked at every night. We'll see you here in two weeks with those bloods. If the knee blows up or you stop passing water, come back sooner, don't sit on it.

spec.situation: Older diabetic with kidney disease on review; creatinine and eGFR read aloud; takes ibuprofen from a shop against advice; ramipril continued, painkiller advice changed.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

bad.reason: Kidney review is stated, but patient does not explicitly report existing kidney disease.
Transcript mentions earlier hospital test, but not that the patient requested it.
bad.text: Earlier kidney function test (type=laboratory, status=completed, requested_by=patient)

bad.reason: Earlier borderline sugar is mentioned, but not that the patient requested the test.

omissions.text: Negative finding not recorded: no blood in the urine/haematuria.
Paracetamol maximum clarified as eight 500 mg tablets in 24 hours ('eight is the ceiling').
Diabetes history detail missing: patient said diabetes started when he was 64 years old.
Investigation result values missing: creatinine was 148 and eGFR was 38 on today's bloods.
Weight trend detail missing: nurse stated last recorded weight in March was 68 kg.
